title: Bank account & phone contract
intro:
A bank account and a phone number are the next two things you need, and each tends to ask for the other. Many newcomers solve this by getting a data SIM or eSIM first, or by using a number arranged through their workplace or school.

**Banks.** You will need your residence card (with your registered address), a Japanese phone number, and sometimes proof of employment or study. Some banks also ask for a personal seal ({印鑑[いんかん]}), though many now accept a signature. Some banks are stricter with people who have only just arrived, so ask before you go. Japan Post Bank ({ゆうちょ銀行[ぎんこう]}) is a common first choice because it has branches and ATMs almost everywhere. Expect to be asked why you are opening the account; this is a routine anti-fraud check. Your cash card is usually sent to your registered address by registered mail, which is not forwarded.

Your salary will be paid by bank transfer ({振込[ふりこみ]}), and many bills can be paid by automatic debit ({口座[こうざ]振替[ふりかえ]}).

**Phones.** There are a few large carriers, their cheaper sub-brands, and many low-cost providers ({格安[かくやす]SIM}). Bring your residence card and a payment method; some providers require a credit card. Early cancellation penalties are much smaller than they once were, but always ask.

Important: never sell, lend or hand over your bank account or SIM to anyone, even when you leave Japan. This is a crime, and such accounts are used for fraud. Close them properly before you go.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 口座[こうざ]を開設[かいせつ]したいんですが。
dialogue.en: I'd like to open an account.

dialogue.en: Certainly. Do you have your residence card and a document showing your employer?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: はい、在留[ざいりゅう]カードと社員証[しゃいんしょう]があります。

dialogue.speaker: Teller
dialogue.jp: ありがとうございます。口座[こうざ]のご利用[りよう]目的[もくてき]を伺[うかが]ってもよろしいでしょうか。
dialogue.en: Thank you. May I ask what you'll use the account for?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 給料[きゅうりょう]の受[う]け取[と]りと、生活費[せいかつひ]の支払[しはら]いです。

tips: Make sure your name is on your mailbox before the cash card is sent, or the registered mail may be returned.
ATM fees can depend on the time of day and whether you use your own bank's machine. Convenience store ATMs are handy but often charge.
Bank account names are usually registered in katakana. Know how your name is written so you can give it to your employer for salary payments.
If someone offers to buy your bank account or phone line when you leave Japan, refuse. It is illegal and you can be held responsible.
Before leaving Japan, cancel your phone contract and close or settle your bank account, but keep one account open until your final salary and any refunds have arrived.
